THE COURT:
When
I issued these oral reasons for judgment, I reserved the right to edit them as
to grammar, background and citations should a transcript be ordered. I have
made such edits, without affecting the substance or final disposition.

[
2
]

The application before the court today is
brought by the defendant, British Columbia Securities Commission (the “Commission")
to strike the notice of civil claim as filed by the plaintiff.

Background

[
3
]

By way of background, in 2016 the plaintiff
entered into a settlement agreement with the Commission in which he admitted
that he had engaged in illegal distribution and unregistered trading and agreed
to a two‑year prohibition arising from that settlement.

[
4
]

On November 4, 2020, a notice of hearing
was filed and issued by the executive director of the Commission alleging that
the plaintiff and a corporate entity had contravened the

Securities Act,

R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418 (the “
Securities Act
”) by failing to disclose his
regulatory history to investors, namely that settlement, and that he had
breached the settlement order by acting as a director of a company when he was
prohibited from doing so, those reasons being indexed at
Dunn (Re)
,
2020
BCSECCOM 449
.

[
5
]

On January 29, 2021, the Commission issued
an order (the “Preservation Order”) preserving approximately $20,000 that had
been held in a bank account in the plaintiff's name. On October 1, 2021, the
Court of Appeal released a decision in an unrelated action with a new
articulation of the evidentiary standard for preservation orders issued by the
Commission, those being indexed at
Party A v. British Columbia (Securities
Commission)
,
2021 BCCA 358
. As a result of those findings, the plaintiff
successfully appealed the Preservation Order, with the Court of Appeal
directing on April 8, 2022 that the Preservation Order be revoked.

[
6
]

Subsequently, on November 24, 2022 the
Commission released its liability decision finding the plaintiff liable in
respect of the allegations raised in the notice of hearing. Thereafter, the
sanction hearing was heard, with an administrative penalty of $60,000 being
ordered along with a market ban for a period of seven years.

[
7
]

The plaintiff appealed the sanctions decision
but not the liability decision. He also later sought to vary the orders arising
from the sanction hearing. That application was refused on June 25, 2024.

[
8
]

The plaintiff then filed this action on
September 26, 2024.

[
9
]

The basis for the claim, as the notice of civil claim
is drafted, is based primarily on the Preservation Order and the effect of its
issuance upon him. However, during submissions, the plaintiff raised issues
that were broader than those arising from the Preservation Order alone.

[
10
]

Regardless, the Commission seeks to strike the notice of civil claim
under R. 9‑5(1)(a) on the basis that the claim discloses no
reasonable cause of action and is an abuse of process, including by virtue of
it being barred by
s. 6(1)
of the
Limitation Act,
S.B.C. 2012, c. 13
(the “
Limitation Act
”).

[
11
]

One of the arguments as to why the claim discloses no reasonable
cause of action arises from the provisions of the
Securities Act
itself,
including specifically a privative clause at
s. 170
, and the statutory
provision regarding the appeal rights,
s. 167(1)
.

S. 170 of the
Securities Act

[
12
]

Specifically, s. 170 states that no action lies against the
Commission for any act done in good faith in performance of the Commission’s duty
or exercise of power. The Commission argues that all of the decisions made
under the
Securities Act
relating to the plaintiff fall under that
category, there being no express reference in the notice of civil claim to the
Commission having acted in bad faith.

[
13
]

The plaintiff argues that he is in fact claiming
that the Commission acted in bad faith, notwithstanding that there is no express
statement to that effect in the notice of civil claim. The entirety of the
facts as set out in the notice of civil claim are as follows:

1.         On November 5, 2020, the British
Columbia Securities Commission issued Citation:
2020 BCSECCOM 449
, Notice of
Hearing against Patrick Dunn and Viribus Structural Connectors Inc.

2.         On January 29, 2021, the British
Columbia Securities Commission issued COR#2021/004, a preservation order
("Dunn Preservation Order"), freezing the Plaintiffs assets.

3.         On April 8, 2022, the British
Columbia Court of Appeal in Dunn v. British Columbia (Securities Commission),

2022 BCCA 132
revoked the Dunn Preservation Order finding that the order was
improperly applied and caused undue harm.

4.         On May 18, 2023, the British
Columbia Securities Commission issued Citation: Dunn,
2023 BCSECCOM 251
. which
prohibited the Plaintiff under section 161(1)(d)(ii) of the Securities Act from
acting as a director or officer of any issuer or registrant, and imposed an
administrative penalty of $60,000 under section 162, which the Plaintiff has
already paid.

5.         On
June 13, 2024, at 4:06 p.m., Catherine Palmer. Senior Enforcement Officer,
confirmed by email that the Plaintiff had paid the monetary sanction of $60,000
and interest of $4,521.54. The email further inquired about plans to pay on
behalf of Viribus, implying a potential breach of the Plaintiffs sanctions.

[
14
]

After setting out the relief sought as being an
order to set aside all sanctions imposed by the Commission and damages for loss
of legal representation, financial losses, emotional distress, loss of
opportunity, breach of rights and costs, the
entirety
of the legal basis is:

1.         Loss of Access to Legal
Representation: Due to the preservation order, the Plaintiff was unable to
secure legal counsel during the critical early stages of the hearing, affecting
his ability to defend himself.

2.         Financial Losses: The
preservation order caused the Plaintiff to miss payments and lose business
opportunities, leading to financial hardship due to frozen accounts.

3.         Emotional Distress: The freezing
of the Plaintiff's accounts caused severe emotional distress and affected his
daily living and defense preparations.

4.         Costs of Litigation: The
Plaintiff incurred substantial costs in fighting the preservation order in the
Supreme Court, including legal fees and related expenses.

5.         Loss of Opportunity: The
Plaintiff missed out on both business and personal opportunities due to the preservation
order.

6.         Breach
of Rights: The BCSC's actions, including the imposition of sanctions.
constituted a breach of the Plaintiff's right to a fair hearing and access to
legal representation, as well as a breach of his legal rights under the British
Columbia Securities Act.

[
15
]

The plaintiff argued that the finding of the Court of Appeal that
the Preservation Order caused undue harm is the basis for his bad faith claim. However,
the Court of Appeal made no such finding. This court is not to take as true
something verifiably untrue. As noted in
Young v. Borzoni
,
2007 BCCA 16
,
at para.
26
in citing para. 27 of
Attn. Gen. of Can. v. Inuit
Tapirisat,
1980 CanLII 21 (S.C.C.)
, notwithstanding that the material facts
in a claim are to be taken as true for the purpose of determining whether a
reasonable cause of action is disclosed, there is no violation of that rule
where the allegation is incapable of proof, for example when it is based on
speculation or an assumption, or not taken as proven. That statement, even if
it rose to the level suggested by the plaintiff, which I do not find it to have
done, is clearly disproven.

[
16
]

The plaintiff also argues that the bad faith claim arises from the
freezing of the accounts, which among other things prevented him from being
able to defend himself.

[
17
]

As currently framed without any plea as to bad faith enumerated
therein, it is plain and obvious that the claim is bound to fail by virtue of
s. 170 of the
Securities Act.

[
18
]

Having made that finding, I will address further in these Reasons
whether the appropriate remedy is to strike the notice of claim on that basis,
or whether there ought to be an opportunity given to the plaintiff to amend his
claim.

S.167 of the
Securities Act

[
19
]

S. 167(1) of the
Securities Act
provides that the plaintiff,
as a person directly affected by a decision of the Commission, has the remedy
of appealing to the Court of Appeal.

[
20
]

The Commission argues that pursuant to s. 167 of the
Securities
Act,
by not seeking leave to appeal the liability decision and having had
his appeals of the sanction decision, and attempts to vary it, dismissed, this
action is nothing more than a renewed effort to avoid the consequences of those
decisions which have now been fully reviewed and appealed in accordance with
the process available under the
Securities Act.
In other words, this
claim is nothing more than a collateral attack on those decisions.

[
21
]

I agree with the Commission that this action is an impermissible
collateral attack to the judicial review and appeal process already undertaken,
or available to have been undertaken. The plaintiff seeks to relitigate issues
that have already been decided, which is impermissible collateral attack under
the doctrine of issue estoppel, as noted in
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E.,
Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 SCR 77, at paras.
25 to 27
.

[
22
]

As noted in
Ajvazi v. Century 21 Prudential Estates (RMD) Ltd.
,

2024 BCSC 276
(“
Ajvazi
”), at para.
53
, bringing a series of
successive related proceedings is an abuse of process even if the plaintiff
generally believes that earlier decisions were wrong or unfairly reached.

[
23
]

Further, as noted in
Garland v. Consumers' Gas Co.
,
2004 SCC
25 (CanLII)
, [2004] 1 SCR 629, at para.
71
, a claim is a collateral attack
if it undermines previous orders issued by a court or administrative tribunal,
invoked where a party is attempting to challenge the validity of an order in
the wrong forum when the party has not used the direct attack procedures
available to them.

[
24
]

The court in
Kamoto Holdings Ltd. v. Village of Nakusp (Village)
,

2020 BCSC 606
, citing
0742848 BC Ltd. v. Squamish (District)
,
2017 BCSC
2177
, noted at para.
50
that this applies even if a plaintiff claims
damages which would otherwise be unavailable on a judicial review.

[
25
]

In both
Kamoto, supra
and
Squamish, supra
, notably the
court was also dealing with applications to strike claims for damages brought
on the basis of injuries alleged to have been suffered as a result of administrative
decisions, those being the refusal to approve a subdivision on the one hand,
and the failure to disclose policies under the building code on the other,
where the decisions themselves were subject to their own judicial review and/or
appeal processes.

[
26
]

That is the case here.

[
27
]

I find that the claims are a collateral attack on the Commission's
determinations in the first instance, as well as the judicial review and appeal
processes available under the
Securities Act,
notwithstanding that those
processes did not allow for a claim in damages as now being sought.

Other Issues

[
28
]

I will also just comment quickly as to some of the procedural‑fairness
issues that the plaintiff raised today during his argument, in terms of those
other processes. Those arguments are ones that were or should have been raised
during the appeal process itself, and variation application, and in that
respect would be also unavailable to argued here under the doctrine of
issue
estoppel,
as being issues that were, our ought to have been, decided in
those proceedings.

[
29
]

Finally, and as a general comment, the
Commission argues that there is no actionable legal wrong particularized in the
notice of civil claim. In this respect, there are no material facts in either the
notice of civil claim or, for that matter, in the plaintiff's response to this
application, that support a specific or enumerated cause of action.

[
30
]

In
Johnson v. Smith
,
2018 BCSC 836
, the
court summarized the circumstances in which a pleading may be struck:

[11]

In
Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union
,
2006 BCSC 750
,
Madam Justice Garson, as she then was, summarized the wide variety of
circumstances in which a pleading will be struck out pursuant to what is now
Rule 9-5, at para. 17:

[17]      In summary, a
pleading will be struck out if:

(a)
the pleadings are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to understand [
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999
CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.)];

(b)
the pleadings do not establish a cause of action and do not advance a claim
known in law (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform
,
supra
);

(c)
the pleadings are without substance in that they are groundless, fanciful and
trifle with the Court’s time (
Borsato v. Basra
, [2000 BCSC 28];

(d)
the pleadings are not bona fides, are oppressive and are designed to cause the
Defendants anxiety, trouble and expense (
Borsato v. Basra
,
supra
);

(e)   the action is brought for
an improper purpose, particularly the harassment and oppression of the
Defendants (
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,
2002 BCSC 466
).

[
31
]

The plaintiff argues that his “general cause of action is
negligence”. However, in order to form a cause of action based on negligence,
the proper elements must be pled, none of which are in the current iteration of
the notice of civil claim.

Limitation Act
Defence

[
32
]

Notwithstanding these findings, particularly with respect to the
argument under s. 170 of the
Securities Act
and general failure to plead
an actionable cause of action, I will also consider the
Limitation Act

defence raised by the Commission, as that will guide whether or not it would be
appropriate to strike the claim or provide the plaintiff with an opportunity to
cure these defects, specifically with respect to any cause of action that the
plaintiff argues at this application that he may have in tort, such as
negligence, or as a result of a claim that the Commission acted in bad faith.

[
33
]

The Commission submits that the plaintiff’s discoverability
of any claim he may have had is governed by
s. 8
of the
Limitation Act
, and
that it had to have been discovered no later than the date on which the Court
of Appeal revoked the Preservation Order, that being April 8, 2022. As
such, the time to file the claim would have expired on April 8, 2024.

[
34
]

As noted above, the legal basis raised by the
plaintiff for his claims is that the Preservation Order made it that he was
unable to secure legal counsel, that it caused him to miss payments and lose
business opportunities, leading to financial hardship, caused emotional
distress, and that he incurred substantial costs in fighting the Preservation
Order.

[
35
]

Those losses and opportunities would have arisen prior and up to the
Preservation Order being set aside, i.e. sometime after its filing in January
of 2021 until it was revoked. Thus, I agree that the losses and the actionable wrong
(if there is one, I make no finding in that regard) would have been
discoverable when the Court of Appeal revoked the Preservation Order.

[
36
]

As to the allegations of bad faith that the plaintiff indicated during
submissions today that he wishes to raise to overcome
s. 170
, the plaintiff
claims the bad faith arose from the freezing of the accounts as a result of the
Preservation Order. However, he argues that the extent of the damages he
suffered as a result of being unable defend himself were not discoverable until
the results of the sanction decision were known, bringing himself within the
two‑year limitation period.

[
37
]

However, it is difficult to accept that any such wrong, namely his
inability to defend himself through the loss of the $20,000 that had been
frozen in that account, as a result of the Preservation Order, was not known
when the Preservation Order was revoked.

[
38
]

The plaintiff knew on April 8, 2022 that the Preservation Order was
revoked. While the liability hearing dates pre-dated that determination, the
submission were not completed until afterwards, that being on May 20, 2022,
such that counsel could have been retained and sought leave to make further
submissions if necessary. There is no evidence or suggestion that the defendant
could not do that for some reason.  In addition, notably, no appeal was taken
of the liability decision. In terms of the sanctions decision, that hearing was
conducted on April 17, 2023, well after the Preservation Order was set aside
and with more than sufficient time for the plaintiff to have been able to
engage counsel.

[
39
]

This notice of civil claim was filed on
September 26, 2024, well after April 8, 2024. I agree that the limitation
period has lapsed such that the claim is bound to fail.

Opportunity to Cure any Defects
before Striking Claim

[
40
]

Turning then to the remedy for the defects in
the notice of civil claim and, specifically, whether or not an appropriate
opportunity ought to be given to the plaintiff to amend his claim.

[
41
]

Given my finding as to
s. 167
and that the
matter is barred by virtue of the
Limitation Act
,
there is no benefit to
allowing an opportunity to amend.

[
42
]

At para. 54 of
Ajvazi,
the guiding
principles to providing such an opportunity were described as follows:

[54] When a
notice of civil claim is inadequately drafted, then a party will generally be
given an opportunity to re‑draft it. However, where it is plain and
obvious that a re‑drafted pleading is bound to fail as it does not raise
an arguable issue, then a party will not be granted the opportunity to re‑draft:

Strata Plan LMS3259 v. Sze Hang Holdings Ltd.
,
2009 BCSC 473
, at para.

40
. Leave to amend is not appropriate in cases where allowing that to occur
would violate the principles of judicial economy, consistency and finality, and
would undermine the integrity of the administration of justice:
Stein v
Keebler
,
2019 BCSC 1338
, at para.
28
.

[
43
]

To allow an amendment to fix the defects would completely disregard
judicial economy.

[
44
]

As such, I grant the application on the terms as sought, and strike
the notice of civil claim under R. 9‑5, without leave to amend, with
costs to the Commission.

[
45
]

I dispense with approval as to form of the order by the plaintiff.

“Associate Judge Robertson”
